title: Manoj Bajpayee Just Made a Film About the Week India Almost Went Bankrupt. It Opens Today.
excerpt: Governor revisits the secret 1991 gold airlift that saved India from collapse — and it's the origin story every NRI never knew they needed.
body:
There's a scene early in **Governor** where the camera lingers on a number. Not a face, not a weapon, not a love interest — a number. India's foreign exchange reserves, somewhere in the neighbourhood of $1.2 billion. Enough to cover roughly two weeks of imports. The country is, for all practical purposes, about to bounce a cheque to the entire world.

<youtube></youtube>

It's 1991. The Gulf War has sent oil prices spiralling. The government is a revolving door — Rajiv Gandhi has been assassinated, a caretaker prime minister is keeping the seat warm, and nobody in the corridors of power wants to make the call that could either save India or sink it. That call falls to one man: the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India.

**Manoj Bajpayee** plays A. Ramanan, a character inspired by the real-life **S. Venkitaramanan**, the RBI Governor who orchestrated what might be the most audacious financial rescue in modern Indian history. The mission: secretly airlift over 60 tonnes of India's gold reserves — first to the Bank of England, then to the Union Bank of Switzerland — as collateral to secure emergency loans. If the world found out before the deal closed, India's credit rating would crater. If the plan failed, 900 million people would wake up in a country that couldn't pay for its own oil.

> "The biggest lessons come from home." — Manoj Bajpayee on his favourite scene in the film

Director **Chinmay D. Mandlekar** — a titan of Marathi cinema making his Hindi directorial debut — frames this economic thriller not as a history lecture but as a heist. The gold has to move. The politicians have to be convinced. The bureaucrats have to hold their nerve. And Bajpayee, who has spent decades proving he can carry absolutely anything, does something remarkable here: he gets quieter as the stakes get louder. His Ramanan is not a shouter. He's the man in the room who knows the math, and the math is terrifying.

The film opens with footage of Sri Lanka's 2022 economic collapse — citizens rioting, fuel lines stretching for miles — before pulling us back three decades to an India that was frighteningly close to the same fate. It's a sharp directorial choice. It says: *this isn't ancient history. This is what failure looks like, and we were right there.*

**Adah Sharma** plays Aditi Verma, a journalist whose narration anchors the non-linear structure. She's fierce and determined, and Sharma brings genuine conviction to a role that could have easily become a plot device. **Madhoo** — yes, *that* Madhoo, the Roja star — returns to Hindi cinema as Ramanan's wife, providing the emotional warmth that keeps the film from becoming a spreadsheet with background music. **Noushad Mohamed Kunju** is excellent as C. Rangarajan, the Deputy Governor who becomes Ramanan's co-conspirator in the gold operation.

The cinematography by **Vishal Sinha** is atmospheric and restrained — all wood-panelled offices, dimly lit corridors, and the kind of government buildings where the air conditioning never quite works. The production design nails the early-90s aesthetic without turning it into a costume party. These are real rooms where real decisions were made.

Is the film perfect? No. The first half can feel dry — Filmfare's review pointedly asks whether a film about a government doing its job constitutes compelling cinema. The music by Mannan Shaah is forgettable, and there's a valid question about whether Bajpayee was the right actor to play a Tamil bureaucrat when accomplished South Indian actors might have brought more cultural specificity to the role. But Bollywood Hungama calls it a "terrific performance," IndiaForums gives it 3.5 stars, and the user ratings are running at 4.3 out of 5. The consensus is clear: Bajpayee elevates everything he touches, and this is no exception.

## Why Every NRI Needs to See This

Here's the thing nobody talks about: the 1991 crisis is the origin story of the Indian diaspora as we know it. The liberalization that followed — under **Manmohan Singh** as Finance Minister — didn't just save India from default. It opened the economy, birthed the IT revolution, created Infosys and Wipro and TCS as global forces, and sent millions of Indians to Silicon Valley, London, Toronto, and Dubai. If you're reading this from a tech job in the Bay Area or a consulting firm in New York, the decisions made in the rooms this film depicts are, in a very real sense, the reason you're there.

Governor takes that story and makes it personal. It puts a face on the anonymous bureaucrats who moved gold across continents in the dead of night so that India could keep its lights on. It's not glamorous. It's not loud. But it might be the most important Indian story of the year.

**Governor** is in theatres now on approximately 750 screens across India. For diaspora audiences, keep an eye on international screening announcements — a film this rooted in the NRI origin story deserves to be seen in every city with a Little India.
